title: Exercise Bank
intro: 14 real contest questions. Pick a skill, then a question — easiest first. Work on paper, then check. Wrong answers get a clue about the *trap* you fell into, not just a red cross.

questions.text: Tian measured her steps and found that it took her 625 steps to walk 500 m. If she walks 10 000 steps at this same rate, what distance will she walk?
hints: This is a rate: **metres per step**. What is the one number you need to find first?
Distance for ONE step = 500 m ÷ 625 steps.
That is 0.8 m per step. Now scale up: 10 000 steps × 0.8 m — then change metres into km.

traps.1: 6.25 looks a lot like 625 — it copies the digits from the question. Find the metres per step and calculate instead.

solution: Shortcut: 625 × 16 = 10 000, so she walks 16 × 500 m = 8 000 m.
questions.idea: Rate → find the amount for ONE, then scale.

questions.text: Mateo and Sydney win a contest. As his prize, Mateo receives $20 every hour for one week. As her prize, Sydney receives $400 every day for one week. What is the difference in the total amounts of money that they receive over the one week period?
hints: Get both prizes in the same unit: **dollars per week**.
How many hours are in one week? (24 × 7)
Mateo: 168 hours × $20. Sydney: 7 days × $400. Then subtract.

traps.1: That’s far too small. Mateo is paid “every hour for one week” — that’s a LOT of hours. How many hours are in a week?

questions.idea: Make both amounts use the same time unit before comparing.

questions.text: At the Gaussian Store, puzzles cost $10 each or $50 for a box of 6 puzzles. If a customer would like exactly 25 puzzles, what is the minimum possible cost?
hints: A box costs $50 ÷ 6 ≈ $8.33 per puzzle — cheaper than buying singles. So use boxes as much as you can…
…but you need **exactly** 25. How many full boxes fit into 25? (6 × 4 = 24)
Compare: 4 boxes + 1 single, or 3 boxes + 7 singles. Which is cheaper?

traps.2: $250 is 5 boxes — that’s 30 puzzles, and she wants exactly 25.
traps.4: $200 is just 4 boxes = 24 puzzles. One puzzle short!

solution: Box price per puzzle: $50 ÷ 6 ≈ $8.33, better than $10. Use as many boxes as possible.
Check the others: 3 boxes + 7 singles = $150 + $70 = $220 (more). 5 boxes would be 30 puzzles — not allowed.
questions.idea: Compare unit prices, then check what the exact total allows.

questions.text: At 9 a.m., Ryan had finished cutting [[1/2]] of his lawn. At 10 a.m., he had finished cutting [[7/8]] of his lawn. If Ryan cut his lawn at a constant rate, at what time did he finish?
hints: From 9 to 10 he did [[7/8]] − [[1/2]] of the lawn. That is his rate **per hour**.
[[7/8]] − [[4/8]] = [[3/8]] of the lawn each hour. How much is left at 10 a.m.?
[[1/8]] is left. If [[3/8]] takes 60 minutes, how long does [[1/8]] take?

traps.3: 10:30 would mean he cuts [[1/8]] in half an hour — but he cuts [[3/8]] per hour, so [[1/8]] only takes a third of an hour.

solution: Rate: [[7/8]] − [[1/2]] = [[3/8]] of the lawn per hour.
[[1/8]] is a third of [[3/8]], so it takes 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes.
questions.idea: Find the rate from two snapshots, then time what’s left.

questions.text: Adam is a cake supplier. He got an order to supply 26 large cakes and 800 cupcakes for a birthday party. The kitchen was available only for 3 hours. Each chef could make either 2 large cakes or 35 cupcakes every hour. During any hour, chefs may work on cakes or cupcakes and then switch for later hour(s), if needed. Adam hired the minimum number of chefs needed to prepare the order. How many chefs did he hire?
hints: Count in **chef-hours**: one chef working for one hour is 1 chef-hour.
Cakes need 26 ÷ 2 = 13 chef-hours. Cupcakes need 800 ÷ 35 ≈ 22.9 chef-hours — and you can’t hire 0.9 of a chef-hour, so round **up**.
13 + 23 = 36 chef-hours in total. They all have to fit into 3 hours.

traps.0: 11 comes from rounding down. If you round down, some cupcakes never get made — when you need *enough*, round UP.
traps.4: 36 is the number of chef-**hours**. You have 3 hours to spread them over, so how many chefs is that?

questions.idea: Turn “who does what” into one number: chef-hours.

questions.text: A map has a scale of 1 : 600 000. On the map, the distance between Gausstown and Piville is 2 cm. What is the actual distance between the towns?
hints: 1 : 600 000 means 1 cm on the map is 600 000 cm in real life.
2 cm on the map → 2 × 600 000 = 1 200 000 cm in real life.
Now convert: 100 cm = 1 m, and 1000 m = 1 km. So 100 000 cm = 1 km.

traps.1: Check your zeros! 1 km is 100 000 cm (five zeros), not 1 000 000 cm.

questions.idea: A scale is a ratio: multiply, then convert the units.

questions.text: The measures of a triangle’s three interior angles are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 7. What are the measures of the angles?
hints: Count the parts: 1 + 4 + 7.
The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. So all 12 parts together make 180°.
One part = 180° ÷ 12. Then multiply for each angle.

traps.0: Check the ratio: 120 ÷ 12 = 10, not 7. These angles are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 10.
traps.1: 10 : 40 : 70 is exactly 1 : 4 : 7 — but those angles only add to 120°. A triangle needs 180°!

questions.idea: Count the parts, then share the whole.

questions.text: A bag contains red, blue, green and orange marbles. The red marbles represent [[1/3]] of the total number of marbles, the blue marbles represent [[1/5]] of the total number of marbles and the green marbles represent [[2/7]] of the total number of marbles. If the bag contains as few marbles as possible, how many orange marbles are there?
hints: You can’t have [[1/3]] of a marble. The total has to be a number you can split into thirds, fifths **and** sevenths.
The smallest such number is 3 × 5 × 7 = 105.
Of 105 marbles: red = 35, blue = 21, green = 30. Orange is what’s left.

traps.4: 35 is the number of RED marbles. The question asks for orange.

solution: The total must be divisible by 3, 5 and 7. Smallest: 3 × 5 × 7 = 105.
questions.idea: Make the whole a number every fraction can share.

questions.text: The grocery receipt shows the cost of three items before tax is added. When a 5% tax is added to the cost of the items, what is the total cost for the three items?
hints: First add up the three prices.
Adding 5% tax means multiplying by 1.05.

traps.0: Not quite — work out the exact total: add the three prices first, then add 5% of that total (tax is charged on the **whole** bill).

solution: (5% of $15 is $0.75 — the same answer, two ways.)

questions.text: Gaussville’s soccer team won 40% of their first 40 games. They went on to win *n* games in a row. At this point, they had won 50% of the total games they had played. What is the value of *n*?
hints: How many games did they win out of the first 40? (40% of 40)
After *n* more wins, wins = 16 + *n* and games played = 40 + *n*. They want wins to be exactly half of games.
Try *n* = 8: is 24 out of 48 equal to 50%?

traps.0: 4 is the gap between 16 wins and 20 (half of 40). But every new win also adds a game to the total, so the target keeps moving — you need more than 4.
traps.1: Test it: 16 + 10 = 26 wins out of 50 games is 52%, a bit too high.

solution: After n wins in a row: (16 + n) wins out of (40 + n) games.
50% means wins = half the games: 16 + n = ½(40 + n) → 32 + 2n = 40 + n → **n = 8**.
Insight: they are 4 wins behind 50%. Each new win closes the gap by only ½ (it adds one win but also one game), so 4 ÷ ½ = 8.
questions.idea: Percent of a changing total: write part ÷ total, compare with the target.

questions.text: For 30 consecutive days, the daily high temperature was recorded. On each of the first 25 days, the temperature recorded was 21°C. On each of the remaining 5 days, the temperature recorded was 15°C. For the 30 days, the mean (average) of the temperatures recorded was
hints: Mean = total ÷ count. Find the total of all 30 temperatures first.
Total = 600. Now divide by 30.

traps.4: 18 is (21 + 15) ÷ 2 — the average of the two averages. But 21°C happened on 25 days and 15°C on only 5, so 21 should count for much more!

questions.idea: Work with the total, not the average.

questions.text: The mean (average) of the four integers 78, 83, 82, and *x* is 80. Which one of the following statements is true?
hints: Flip it around: sum = mean × count. What must the four numbers add up to?
4 × 80 = 320. The three known numbers add to 78 + 83 + 82.
Find *x*, then compare it with 80.
solution: *x* = 320 − 243 = 77, which is 3 less than the mean (80) → **(D)**.
questions.idea: mean × count = total — always convert to totals first.

questions.text: In a group of seven friends, the mean (average) age of three of the friends is 12 years and 3 months and the mean age of the remaining four friends is 13 years and 5 months. In months, the mean age of all seven friends is
hints: Change everything to months first: 12 y 3 m = 147 months, 13 y 5 m = 161 months.
Total months of the first three: 3 × 147. Total of the other four: 4 × 161.
Add the totals, divide by 7 (the number of friends). Never just average the two averages!

traps.1: 154 is (147 + 161) ÷ 2 — averaging the averages. There are 4 older friends and only 3 younger, so the mean should be a bit closer to 161.

questions.idea: Combining groups: add the totals, add the counts.

questions.text: The mean (average) height of a group of children would be increased by 6 cm if 12 of the children in the group were each 8 cm taller. How many children are in the group?
hints: Think totals. If the mean goes up by 6 for *all n* children, by how much does the **total** go up?
The total goes up by 6 × *n*.
But the total only really changes because 12 children each grew 8 cm: 12 × 8 = 96. So 6 × *n* = 96.
solution: Let there be *n* children. The mean rises by 6, so the total rises by 6 × *n*.
The total rises because 12 children are 8 cm taller: 12 × 8 = 96 cm.
questions.idea: A change in the mean × count = the change in the total.

questions.text: It took Nasrin two hours and thirty minutes to canoe the 4.5 km into her camp. Paddling much faster, the return trip took her [[1/3]] of the time. What was Nasrin’s mean (average) speed as she paddled to camp and back?
hints: Average speed = **total distance ÷ total time**. It is NOT the average of the two speeds.
Going: 2.5 h. Return: [[1/3]] of 2.5 h = [[5/6]] h (50 minutes). What is the total time?
Total distance there and back is 2 × 4.5 = 9 km. Divide by the total time, 3[[1/3]] h.

traps.2: 1.8 km/h is only her speed on the way TO camp (4.5 ÷ 2.5). Average speed uses the whole round trip.

solution: Time out: 2.5 h. Time back: 2.5 ÷ 3 = [[5/6]] h.
Total time: 2.5 + [[5/6]] = [[10/3]] h. Total distance: 4.5 + 4.5 = 9 km.
questions.idea: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

questions.text:
James works for a courier company. He had to deliver 5 parcels. His motorcycle uses 3 litres of fuel to drive 45 km. The tank of the motorcycle holds 12 litres of fuel and was full when he started out.

The motorcycle used one quarter of the fuel for the delivery of the first parcel. For the second and third parcels together, the motorcycle used half of the remaining fuel.

James recognized that the fuel left in the tank after delivering the third parcel was only three fifths of what he needed to deliver the last two parcels. He filled up the tank of his motorcycle and then finished the deliveries.

How far did James travel to deliver the 5 parcels?
hints: First the rate: 45 km per 3 litres is **15 km per litre**. Then just track the litres.
Start 12 L → parcel 1 uses [[1/4]] of 12 = 3 L → 9 L left → parcels 2 & 3 use half of 9 = 4.5 L → 4.5 L left.
4.5 L is [[3/5]] of what the last two parcels need. So they need 4.5 ÷ 3 × 5 = 7.5 L. Add up ALL the fuel used.

traps.0: 180 km would be just 12 L — one tank. But he refilled, so he burned more than one tank’s worth.

solution: Parcel 1: [[1/4]] × 12 = 3 L, leaving 9 L. Parcels 2 & 3: ½ × 9 = 4.5 L, leaving 4.5 L.
4.5 L = [[3/5]] of the need → need = 4.5 × [[5/3]] = 7.5 L for the last two parcels.
Total fuel burned: 3 + 4.5 + 7.5 = 15 L. Distance: 15 × 15 = **225 km** → **(C)**.
questions.idea: Rate = km per litre; then count the litres that were really used.

questions.text: Betty and Ann are walking around a rectangular park with dimensions 600 m by 400 m, as shown. They both begin at the top left corner of the park and walk at constant but different speeds. Betty walks in a clockwise direction and Ann walks in a counterclockwise direction. Points *P, Q, R, S, T* divide the bottom edge of the park into six segments of equal length. When Betty and Ann meet for the first time, they are between *Q* and *R*. Which of the following could be the ratio of Betty’s speed to Ann’s speed?
hints: They walk in opposite directions around the park, so by the time they first meet, together they have covered the whole boundary: 2 × (600 + 400) = 2000 m.
Ann goes down the left side (400 m) and then along the bottom. *Q* is 200 m along the bottom and *R* is 300 m. So Ann has walked between 600 m and 700 m.
Same time → speed ratio = distance ratio. Betty walked 2000 − Ann’s distance, so Betty : Ann is between 1300 : 700 and 1400 : 600. Which option fits?

traps.2: So close! 11 : 6 ≈ 1.83, but the ratio has to be between 1300 : 700 ≈ 1.86 and 1400 : 600 ≈ 2.33. Just under the bottom edge.

solution: Perimeter = 2 × (600 + 400) = 2000 m. Meeting for the first time means their distances add up to 2000 m.
The six segments are 100 m each, so *Q* and *R* are 200 m and 300 m along the bottom. Ann’s distance is 400 + (200 to 300) = 600 m to 700 m.
Betty’s distance is then 1400 m down to 1300 m. Speed ratio = distance ratio, so it lies between 1300 : 700 (≈ 1.86) and 1400 : 600 (≈ 2.33).
questions.idea: Meeting around a loop: the distances add up to one full lap.
